prompt: In a Lewis electron-dot structure, what does a line between two atoms represent?

choices.text: A pair of electrons shared between the atoms: a bond
A lone pair of electrons
choices.why: Lone pairs are drawn as two adjacent dots on one atom. A line is a shared pair: a bond.

choices.text: A single unpaired electron
choices.why: Single valence electrons are drawn as dots. A line stands for two electrons shared between atoms.

choices.text: The distance between the nuclei
choices.why: Lewis structures show connectivity, not distances. A line is a shared electron pair.

explanation: In Lewis diagrams, valence electrons are dots. Two paired electrons on one atom (a lone pair) are two adjacent dots, and two paired electrons shared between atoms (a bond) are drawn as a line.

prompt: What can Lewis structures predict on their own, and what do they need VSEPR for?

choices.text: On their own they show how atoms are connected; with VSEPR they predict the molecule's shape
On their own they predict the full three-dimensional shape
choices.why: Lewis structures are two-dimensional and show only connectivity. Shape needs VSEPR as well.

choices.text: On their own they give exact bond lengths
choices.why: Lewis structures don't give bond lengths. They show connectivity, and with VSEPR they predict shape.

choices.text: They can't show connectivity without VSEPR
choices.why: Connectivity is exactly what Lewis structures show by themselves. VSEPR adds the shape.

explanation: Lewis diagrams show how atoms are connected, and when coupled with valence shell electron pair repulsion theory (VSEPR), they can be used to predict the shape of a molecule.

prompt: Why are hydrogen and helium exceptions to the octet rule?

choices.text: Their valence shell is n = 1, which is full with just two electrons (1s^2)
They are too reactive to complete an octet
choices.why: Helium is famously unreactive. The point is that their n = 1 valence shell holds only two electrons.

choices.text: They don't form bonds at all
choices.why: Hydrogen forms bonds readily. Like other atoms, it bonds to fill its valence shell, which for n = 1 means two electrons.

choices.text: They need more than eight electrons
choices.why: The opposite: their full valence shell has only two electrons.

explanation: H and He have n = 1 as their valence shell, so a full valence shell has only two electrons (1s^2). They still form bonds to achieve a full valence shell, which is why it may be better to think of a "full valence" rule.

prompt: Which of these is an example of hypovalency (fewer than eight valence electrons) in a valid Lewis structure?

choices.text: Boron in BH3, with three bonds and six valence electrons
Sulfur in SF6, with twelve valence electrons
choices.why: That is hypervalency: more than eight electrons.

choices.text: Carbon in CH4, with eight valence electrons
choices.why: Carbon in methane has a full octet.

choices.text: Chlorine in ClF3, with ten valence electrons
choices.why: That is hypervalency, possible for chlorine because it is in the third row.

explanation: Hypovalency is a partially filled valence shell. Boron in BH3 has three bonds and only six valence electrons; a carbocation, with a positive carbon holding six electrons, is another example. Both are strong Lewis acids.

prompt: In the Lewis structure of ClF3, chlorine has three single bonds and two lone pairs. Counting for the octet rule, how many electrons are in chlorine's valence shell?
explanation: For octet counting, every electron associated with the atom counts: unbonded electrons plus 2 per bond. Chlorine has 2 lone pairs (4 electrons) plus 3 bonds (6 electrons) = 10, so it is hypervalent.

prompt: How does counting electrons for the octet rule differ from counting them for formal charge?

choices.text: For octets, an atom gets both electrons of each bond; for formal charge, it gets one per bond
The two counts are done exactly the same way
choices.why: The text warns that the rules are different: octet counting gives an atom both electrons of every bond it shares.

choices.text: For octets, bonding electrons are ignored
choices.why: For octets, all bonded electrons count (2 per bond), along with lone pairs.

choices.text: For formal charge, lone pairs are ignored
choices.why: For formal charge, all unshared electrons are subtracted, and one electron per bond.

explanation: Electrons in an atom's valence (octet) = its unbonded electrons + 2 per bond. Formal charge is different: valence electrons of the free atom − unshared electrons − bonds, which in effect gives the atom one electron from each bond.

prompt: BF3 can be drawn with only single bonds, or in three resonance structures with a B=F double bond. What do the measured B–F bonds show?

choices.text: They are shorter than single bonds but longer than double bonds: some double-bond character
They are pure single bonds, exactly as in the all-single-bond structure
choices.why: The bonds are shorter than single bonds, as the resonance structures with B=F double bonds predict.

choices.text: One is a double bond and two are single bonds
choices.why: All three B–F bonds are the same, intermediate between single and double.

choices.text: They are all full double bonds
choices.why: The bonds are longer than double bonds: the true structure is intermediate.

explanation: Considering all four resonance structures predicts B–F bonds with some double-bond character. That is the case: BF3's bond lengths are shorter than single bonds but longer than double bonds.

prompt: What does the double-headed arrow between resonance structures mean?

choices.text: The actual electronic structure is an average of the structures shown
The molecule switches rapidly back and forth between the structures
choices.why: The molecule doesn't oscillate. The arrow means the real structure is an average of those shown.

choices.text: The structures are in chemical equilibrium
choices.why: Resonance structures aren't different molecules reacting. Together they describe one real structure, their average.

choices.text: The atoms move to new positions in each structure
choices.why: The atoms stay in the same positions; only the electrons are placed differently.

explanation: Resonance structures have the atoms in the same positions but the electrons placed differently. The double-headed arrow indicates that the actual electronic structure is an average of those shown, not that the molecule oscillates between them.

prompt: One Lewis structure of ozone (O3) has one O–O single bond and one O=O double bond. What do measurements of ozone's two bonds show?

choices.text: Both bonds are the same length, between a single and a double bond
One bond is short (double) and the other long (single)
choices.why: That's what a single Lewis structure predicts, but both O–O distances are identical, 127.2 pm.

choices.text: Both are single bonds
choices.why: At 127.2 pm, both bonds are shorter than a typical O–O single bond (148 pm).

choices.text: Both are double bonds, like O2
choices.why: At 127.2 pm, both bonds are longer than the O=O double bond in O2 (120.7 pm).

explanation: Both O–O distances in ozone are 127.2 pm, shorter than a typical O–O single bond (148 pm) and longer than the O=O double bond in O2 (120.7 pm). Ozone is described by two resonance structures, and its real structure is their average.

prompt: How many valence electrons are in the Lewis structure of the sulfate ion, SO4^2−?
explanation: Sulfur has 6 valence electrons, each of the four oxygens has 6, and the 2− charge adds 2: 6 + 4(6) + 2 = 32.

prompt: How many equivalent resonance structures describe the carbonate ion, CO3^2−?

choices.text: Three
Two
choices.why: Ozone has two. Carbonate's double bond can go to any of its three oxygens, giving three.

choices.text: One
choices.why: One structure would predict one short C=O and two longer C–O bonds, but all three C–O bonds are identical.

choices.text: Four
choices.why: Carbonate has three oxygens, so the C=O double bond can be placed in three ways.

explanation: In carbonate, carbon needs one C=O double bond to complete its octet, and it can be made to any of the three oxygens. The actual structure, with three identical C–O bonds, is the average of the three resonance structures.

prompt: The nitrate ion, NO3^−, is described by three resonance structures, each with one N=O double bond and two N–O single bonds. What is the average N–O bond order in the actual structure?
explanation: Across the three structures there are 4 bonds' worth (one double, two single) spread over 3 N–O links: 4/3 ≈ 1.33. That is why nitrate's bonds are somewhat shorter than single bonds.

prompt: Benzene can be drawn as two resonance structures of alternating single and double bonds. What does experiment show about its six C–C bonds?

choices.text: All are identical, 139.9 pm, between a C–C single bond (154 pm) and a C=C double bond (134 pm)
Three are short double bonds and three are long single bonds
choices.why: Each structure predicts that, but they put the double bonds in different places. Measurements show one bond length, intermediate between the two.

choices.text: All are single bonds, 154 pm
choices.why: Benzene's C–C bonds are 139.9 pm, shorter than a single bond.

choices.text: All are double bonds, 134 pm
choices.why: Benzene's C–C bonds are 139.9 pm, longer than a double bond.

explanation: Experimentation shows that each carbon–carbon bond in benzene is identical, at 139.9 pm, intermediate between a typical C–C single bond (154 pm) and C=C double bond (134 pm). The actual electronic structure is an average of the two resonance structures, often drawn as a circle inside the hexagon.

prompt: According to the section's summary, how does the number of resonance structures relate to stability?

choices.text: A molecule with several resonance structures is more stable than one with fewer
More resonance structures make a molecule less stable
choices.why: The summary says the opposite: delocalization over several resonance structures makes a molecule more stable.

choices.text: The number of resonance structures has nothing to do with stability
choices.why: The summary links them: a molecule with several resonance structures is more stable than one with fewer.

explanation: The net sum of valid resonance structures, the resonance hybrid, represents the overall delocalization of electrons. A molecule that has several resonance structures is more stable than one with fewer, though some resonance structures are more favorable than others.

prompt: Which atom can be hypervalent, with more than eight electrons in its valence shell?

choices.text: Sulfur
Fluorine
choices.why: Fluorine is in the second row (n = 2) and cannot have more than eight valence electrons.

choices.text: Carbon
choices.why: Carbon is in the second row. Five or more bonds are nearly unheard of for atoms with n ≤ 2.

choices.text: Nitrogen
choices.why: Nitrogen is in the second row, where a full valence shell is an octet.

explanation: Atoms with n ≥ 3, like sulfur, have additional subshells in the valence shell and can have more than eight electrons, as in SF6. Five or more bonds are nearly unheard of for atoms with n ≤ 2.

prompt: In the Lewis structure of SF6, sulfur makes six single bonds and has no lone pairs. How many electrons are in sulfur's valence shell?
explanation: Six bonds × 2 electrons per bond = 12 valence electrons on sulfur, which makes it hypervalent.

prompt: What is the current consensus about d orbitals in the bonding of hypervalent molecules like SF6?

choices.text: d orbitals are not significantly involved; their small participation is about the same as in SF4 and SF2
SF6 bonds by fully using sulfur's 3d orbitals, as Pauling proposed
choices.why: That was the older idea. MO and VB theory both show d orbitals are no more involved in SF6 than in SF4 and SF2.

choices.text: d orbitals are involved in SF6 but not at all in SF4 or SF2
choices.why: All three have a small and roughly identical participation of d orbitals in their wavefunctions.

choices.text: Hypervalency is fully explained by wave mechanics using d orbitals
choices.why: The text says the idea that d orbitals are involved in bonding isn't accurate according to wave mechanics.

explanation: Chemists like Pauling once thought hypervalence came from expanded octets using d orbitals. The consensus now, from both MO and VB theory, is that d orbitals are no more involved in SF6 than in SF4 and SF2. Hybrid orbitals with d contributions remain a useful language for describing geometries.

prompt: According to the section, how should bonding theories such as hybridization be judged?

choices.text: By their predictions, compared with experimental evidence
By how simple and intuitive they are
choices.why: The section's rule is that bonding theories can only be judged by their predictions, checked against empirical evidence.

choices.text: By whether they describe what is "really" happening
choices.why: The section sidesteps that question: a theory is good to the extent that its predictions match experiment.

choices.text: By how old and established they are
choices.why: Age doesn't decide it: bonding theories can only be judged by their predictions.

explanation: Bonding theories can only be judged by their predictions. Hybridization predicts the shapes of PF5 and SF6 well, but calculated energies from it can be off by tens of kcal/mol. When a theory gives a wrong answer, at least one of its assumptions doesn't hold.

prompt: Using formal charge = (valence electrons of the free atom) − (unshared electrons) − (bonds), what is the formal charge on nitrogen in the ammonium ion, NH4^+? (Nitrogen has four N–H bonds and no lone pairs.)
explanation: Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons as a free atom: 5 − 0 unshared − 4 bonds = +1. The four hydrogens are each 1 − 0 − 1 = 0, so the formal charges sum to +1, the charge of the ion.

prompt: In one resonance structure of ozone, a terminal oxygen has one single bond and three lone pairs. What is its formal charge?
explanation: Oxygen has 6 valence electrons as a free atom: 6 − 6 unshared electrons − 1 bond = −1.

prompt: What must the formal charges of all the atoms in a polyatomic ion add up to?

choices.text: The charge of the ion
Zero, always
choices.why: Formal charges add up to zero in a neutral molecule. In an ion they add up to the ion's charge.

choices.text: The number of bonds
choices.why: The check is on charge: the formal charges in an ion sum to the ion's charge, as in ICl4^−, where they sum to −1.

choices.text: The number of valence electrons
choices.why: The sum of formal charges equals the overall charge: zero for a molecule, the ion's charge for an ion.

explanation: The sum of the formal charges of all atoms in a molecule must be zero, and the sum in an ion should equal the charge of the ion: in ICl4^−, iodine is −1 and each Cl is 0, summing to −1.

prompt: In carbon monoxide's Lewis structure, carbon has a formal charge of −1 and oxygen +1. What does this tell you about the actual charges on the atoms?

choices.text: Nothing directly: formal charge is a bookkeeping procedure, not the actual charge
Carbon carries a full −1 charge and oxygen a full +1 charge
choices.why: Formal charge is hypothetical: the charge each atom would have if bonding electrons were shared evenly. It isn't the actual charge.

choices.text: CO is an ionic compound
choices.why: Formal charges come from a bookkeeping rule applied to a Lewis structure; they don't make a molecule ionic.

explanation: Formal charge is the hypothetical charge an atom would have if the electrons in its bonds were shared evenly. It is a useful bookkeeping procedure, but it does not indicate the presence of actual charges.

prompt: In BrCl3, bromine has three single bonds and two lone pairs, and each chlorine has one bond and three lone pairs. What are the formal charges?

choices.text: Bromine 0, each chlorine 0
Bromine +3, each chlorine −1
choices.why: Br: 7 − 4 unshared − 3 bonds = 0. Cl: 7 − 6 − 1 = 0. Every atom is formally neutral.

choices.text: Bromine −1, each chlorine 0
choices.why: That would apply to iodine in ICl4^−, which has four bonds and two lone pairs. Bromine in BrCl3 is 7 − 4 − 3 = 0.

choices.text: Bromine 0, each chlorine −1
choices.why: Each chlorine is 7 − 6 − 1 = 0, and the formal charges of a neutral molecule must sum to zero.

explanation: Br: 7 valence electrons − 4 unshared − 3 bonds = 0. Each Cl: 7 − 6 − 1 = 0. All atoms in BrCl3 have a formal charge of zero, and the total is zero, as it must be in a neutral molecule.

prompt: Lewis structures predict a linear BeF2 molecule. What is BeF2 actually like at room temperature and pressure?

choices.text: A quartz-like solid with four-coordinate, tetrahedral Be in an extended network
A gas of linear BeF2 molecules
choices.why: Linear BeF2 monomers exist only in the vapor, above about 1000 °C at around 1 atm.

choices.text: A gas of BeF2 dimers bridged by fluorine
choices.why: Dimers bridged by halogens describe gaseous BeCl2. At room temperature BeF2 is a solid network.

choices.text: A liquid of linear molecules
choices.why: At room temperature BeF2 is a solid. Even its liquid has a fluctuating tetrahedral structure.

explanation: At ambient temperature and pressure, BeF2 is a solid that looks like quartz, with four-coordinate tetrahedral Be and two-coordinate F in an extended three-dimensional network. Only in the vapor, above 1000 °C, does it exist as linear monomers.

prompt: In the vapor phase, BeF2 is a linear monomer with a Be–F bond length of 1.43 Å, shorter than in the solid (1.54 Å). What is the short bond consistent with?

choices.text: A double bond between Be and F
A weaker bond than in the solid
choices.why: Shorter bonds go with more bonding, not less. The 1.43 Å bond is consistent with a Be=F double bond.

choices.text: An ionic bond with no covalent character
choices.why: The text interprets the short 1.43 Å bond as consistent with a double bond between Be and F.

explanation: In the vapor phase, above 1000 °C, BeF2 exists as a monomer with linear geometry and a bond length of 1.43 Å, consistent with a double bond between Be and F. In the solid, the Be–F bond is 1.54 Å.

prompt: What form does BeCl2 take in the gas phase (below the highest temperatures)?

choices.text: A dimer, with two chlorine atoms bridging two three-coordinate Be atoms
Only linear BeCl2 monomers
choices.why: The linear monomer appears only at higher temperatures in the vapor. Otherwise the gas is a chlorine-bridged dimer.

choices.text: A three-dimensional network like quartz
choices.why: That's solid BeF2. Solid BeCl2 is a one-dimensional chain; gaseous BeCl2 is a dimer.

choices.text: Free Be^2+ and Cl^− ions
choices.why: Gaseous BeCl2 is a dimer with bridging chlorines, not separated ions.

explanation: In the gas phase, BeCl2 exists as a dimer with two chlorine atoms bridging two Be atoms, which are three-coordinate. At higher temperatures the linear monomer also exists. Solid BeCl2 is a one-dimensional polymer of edge-shared tetrahedra.

prompt: How well do Lewis structures and VSEPR predict the real structure of BF3?

choices.text: Well: BF3 is a trigonal planar monomer with bonds shorter than single bonds
Poorly: BF3 is really a dimer, B2F6
choices.why: It's boron trihydride, BH3, that actually exists as a dimer (B2H6). BF3 is a monomer, as predicted.

choices.text: Poorly: BF3 is tetrahedral
choices.why: VSEPR predicts trigonal planar geometry for BF3, and that is what is observed.

choices.text: Poorly: BF3 is a solid network like BeF2
choices.why: BF3 exists as a trigonal planar monomer, just as Lewis structures and VSEPR predict.

explanation: Boron trihalides have properties largely predicted by Lewis structures and VSEPR. BF3 is a trigonal planar monomer, and its resonance hybrid correctly predicts partial double-bond character, a bond shorter than a single bond.

prompt: Why do boron trihalides react readily with Lewis bases?

choices.text: Boron is electron deficient, so they are strong Lewis acids
Boron has extra lone pairs to donate
choices.why: Boron in BX3 has no lone pairs and only six valence electrons in the single-bond structure. It accepts electrons.

choices.text: Boron is hypervalent
choices.why: Boron is in the second row and is electron deficient, not hypervalent.

choices.text: The B–X bonds are nonpolar
choices.why: The B–F bond is highly polarized. The reactivity comes from the electron-deficient boron center.

explanation: Boron trihalides are electron deficient at the boron center and react readily with Lewis bases. In other words, they are strong Lewis acids (electrophiles).

prompt: In its pure form, how does boron trihydride (BH3) actually exist?

choices.text: As a dimer, B2H6, with two hydrogens bridging the borons in 3-center-2-electron bonds
As a stable trigonal planar monomer, as Lewis structures predict
choices.why: The BH3 monomer is not stable. Pure boron trihydride exists as the dimer B2H6.

choices.text: As a dimer held together by B=B double bonds
choices.why: The borons are linked by two bridging hydrogens in 3-center-2-electron bonds, a structure no valid Lewis structure captures.

choices.text: As a solid network like BeF2
choices.why: Pure boron trihydride is a dimeric gas, B2H6.

explanation: The BH3 monomer is not stable, though it can form a stable adduct with a Lewis base. In its pure form it exists as a dimeric gas, B2H6, with two hydrogens bridging the two borons in 3-center-2-electron bonds, which no valid Lewis structure can show.
